title: OEE with Availability, Performance and Quality in DAX using ratios of sums
summary: DAX measures for OEE on a production star schema that stay correct at line and total rows, with a time-weighted quality factor, a control measure, a data-quality check and an ISINSCOPE rank.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- Calculates Availability, Performance, Quality and OEE (Availability x Performance x Quality) as ratios of SUMS, so every
-- cell of a matrix is right: a machine row, a line subtotal and the grand total. The common failure is a calculated column or
-- a measure that stores a percentage per row and then averages it; a half-shift on one machine would then weigh as much as a
-- full week on another. Here the building blocks are minutes and counts that can be added, and the divisions come last.
-- Quality is weighted by ideal time, so the product A x P x Q equals fully productive time / planned production time even when
-- machines or products have different ideal cycle times. A check measure proves it. A rank measure uses ISINSCOPE so that it
-- shows only on machine rows and not on subtotals.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact Production Shift'. GRAIN: one row per machine, per shift, per day and per product run (no two rows for the same
--   machine, shift, day and product). Columns: Date, MachineKey, ProductKey, PlannedMinutes (planned production time: shift
--   length minus planned stops such as breaks and planned maintenance), RunMinutes (time the machine was producing),
--   IdealCycleSec (ideal seconds per unit for that product), TotalCount (all units made, good and bad), GoodCount.
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date, Year, MonthNumber, YearMonth; marked as date table), 'Dim Machine' (MachineKey, Machine, Line, Plant),
--   'Dim Product' (ProductKey, PartNumber, Family).
-- RELATIONSHIPS: each dimension to the fact, one-to-many, single direction (dimension filters fact):
--   'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact Production Shift'[Date]; 'Dim Machine'[MachineKey] -> 'Fact Production Shift'[MachineKey];
--   'Dim Product'[ProductKey] -> 'Fact Production Shift'[ProductKey].
-- Works in Power BI Desktop and in a Fabric semantic model. Name your OEE definition (what counts as planned, what is a loss)
-- in a definition sheet; the model only implements it.

-- ==== Code ====
-- Each block is one measure created with New measure.
Planned Minutes =
SUM ( 'Fact Production Shift'[PlannedMinutes] )

Run Minutes =
SUM ( 'Fact Production Shift'[RunMinutes] )

Total Count =
SUM ( 'Fact Production Shift'[TotalCount] )

Good Count =
SUM ( 'Fact Production Shift'[GoodCount] )

-- Time needed to make all units at ideal speed; iterates the fact rows because the ideal cycle time differs per row
Ideal Run Minutes =
SUMX ( 'Fact Production Shift', 'Fact Production Shift'[TotalCount] * 'Fact Production Shift'[IdealCycleSec] ) / 60

-- Ideal time of the good units only: the 'fully productive' time
Fully Productive Minutes =
SUMX ( 'Fact Production Shift', 'Fact Production Shift'[GoodCount] * 'Fact Production Shift'[IdealCycleSec] ) / 60

Availability =
DIVIDE ( [Run Minutes], [Planned Minutes] )

Performance =
DIVIDE ( [Ideal Run Minutes], [Run Minutes] )

-- Time-weighted quality. Use [Quality (pieces)] if you have one product only and prefer the plain piece ratio.
Quality =
DIVIDE ( [Fully Productive Minutes], [Ideal Run Minutes] )

Quality (pieces) =
DIVIDE ( [Good Count], [Total Count] )

OEE =
VAR A = [Availability]
VAR P = [Performance]
VAR Q = [Quality]
RETURN
    IF ( NOT ISBLANK ( A ) && NOT ISBLANK ( P ) && NOT ISBLANK ( Q ), A * P * Q )

-- Control measure: must equal [OEE] in every cell; if not, a column or relationship is wrong
OEE (check) =
DIVIDE ( [Fully Productive Minutes], [Planned Minutes] )

-- Data quality: fact rows whose ideal time is longer than their run time (performance above 100 percent) point to a wrong
-- ideal cycle time, a counter that was not reset or run minutes that were booked too low
Rows with Performance above 100% =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER (
        'Fact Production Shift',
        'Fact Production Shift'[TotalCount] * 'Fact Production Shift'[IdealCycleSec] / 60 > 'Fact Production Shift'[RunMinutes]
    )
)

-- Target for conditional formatting: example value, set your own from your improvement plan
OEE Target =
0.65

OEE vs Target Status =
VAR Raw = [OEE]
RETURN
    IF ( ISBLANK ( Raw ), BLANK (), IF ( ROUND ( Raw, 4 ) >= [OEE Target], "At or above target", "Below target" ) )

-- Rank only on machine rows. ALLSELECTED keeps slicers (plant, month) but ignores the rows of the visual itself,
-- so the machines are ranked against each other inside the current selection.
OEE Rank (machine) =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Machine'[Machine] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Machine'[Machine] ), [OEE], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- ==== Worked example (small, invented numbers; verified by calculation outside Power BI) ====
-- Two fact rows, one day: Machine A makes Product X (ideal 30 s), Machine B makes Product Y (ideal 60 s).
--   Machine A: Planned 450, Run 400, TotalCount 700, GoodCount 679
--   Machine B: Planned 240, Run 190, TotalCount 160, GoodCount 154
--   Machine A  Planned=450  Run=400  IdealRun=350.0  FullyProductive=339.5  Availability=88.89%  Performance=87.50%  Quality=97.00%  OEE=75.44%
--   Machine B  Planned=240  Run=190  IdealRun=160.0  FullyProductive=154.0  Availability=79.17%  Performance=84.21%  Quality=96.25%  OEE=64.17%
--   Total      Planned=690  Run=590  IdealRun=510.0  FullyProductive=493.5  Availability=85.51%  Performance=86.44%  Quality=96.76%  OEE=71.52%
-- [OEE (check)] gives 71.52% for the total row, equal to [OEE]. Quality (pieces) is 96.86% at the total row; the time-weighted figure differs slightly because the products have different ideal times.
-- The tempting wrong way: average the OEE of the two rows. ((75.44% + 64.17%) / 2 = 69.81%.) The total row of the
-- model above shows 71.52%, because Machine A carried 450 of the 690 planned minutes. The same trap hits Availability: the
-- average of the two row values is 84.03%, the correct total is 85.51%.
-- OEE Rank (machine) shows 1 for Machine A and 2 for Machine B on their rows and blank on the total row.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Replace the table and column names; keep the structure (sums first, divide last).
-- If planned stops are in a separate event table, subtract them inside PlannedMinutes in the data model (Power Query), not in the measure.
-- Several shifts or product runs per machine are fine: the grain only requires that rows can be added.
-- If your OEE definition books changeover or micro-stops differently, change what goes into RunMinutes in the source, not the measures.
-- A line view: put 'Dim Machine'[Line] on rows. Totals stay correct because nothing is averaged.
-- Cap or not: the model does not cap Performance at 100 percent because that hides data errors; use the check measure to find them.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- SUMX over the fact table is the only iteration, over one table with simple multiplication; it is fast even for millions of rows.
-- Keep PlannedMinutes, RunMinutes and the counts as plain columns; avoid calculated columns that store percentages.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Averaging percentages (AVERAGE of a ratio column, or AVERAGEX over machines of [OEE]) instead of dividing the sums.
-- Computing Quality as Good / Total across products with very different ideal times, then expecting A x P x Q to equal the
--   time-based OEE; use the time-weighted quality or one product per view.
-- Mixing planned production time definitions between plants in one report.
-- Using RANKX with ALL ( 'Dim Machine' ) and wondering why slicers have no effect, or without the ISINSCOPE guard and getting
--   a rank of 1 on the total row.
-- Comparing a percentage with a target without rounding: 64.999999 percent is below 65 percent in floating point. Round first.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- The model holds machine and product data, no personal data. Shift names are fine; do not add operator names to a dataset that
--   is shared widely, and agree with the works council how machine and shift figures may be used in performance talks.
-- OEE is an improvement metric. It is not a quality record and not a release of product.

title: Scrap rate, scrap cost and reason share in DAX with REMOVEFILTERS and a safe rank
summary: DAX measures for scrap rate, ppm, cost and the share of each scrap reason on a two-fact star schema, using REMOVEFILTERS on the reason table only and an ISINSCOPE-guarded machine rank, with a checked example.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- Scrap rate, scrap cost and the share of each scrap reason, built so that the percentages are right at every level.
--   Scrap Rate = scrap quantity / produced quantity (produced includes the scrapped units; say so in your definition sheet)
--   Share of reason = scrap of this reason / scrap of all reasons within the current machine, product and date selection
-- The share uses REMOVEFILTERS on the reason dimension only. That clears the reason filter but keeps machine, product and date
-- filters, which is what 'share within the current selection' means. ALL ( 'Fact Scrap' ) would also clear filters that arrive
-- from the related machine, product and date tables and produce shares of the whole plant.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact 1: 'Fact Output'. GRAIN: one row per lot (work order operation) that was produced. Columns: Date, MachineKey, ProductKey, QtyProduced.
-- Fact 2: 'Fact Scrap'. GRAIN: one row per lot and scrap reason. Columns: Date, MachineKey, ProductKey, ReasonKey, ScrapQty.
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Machine' (MachineKey, Machine, Line), 'Dim Product' (ProductKey, PartNumber,
--   StandardCost), 'Dim Scrap Reason' (ReasonKey, Reason, Category).
-- RELATIONSHIPS, all one-to-many from dimension to fact, single direction: Dim Date, Dim Machine and Dim Product each to BOTH facts;
--   'Dim Scrap Reason' to 'Fact Scrap' only. There is deliberately no relationship between 'Dim Scrap Reason' and 'Fact Output'.
-- Consequence: with a reason on the rows, [Produced Qty] does not change from row to row, so [Scrap Rate] per reason is that reason's
-- contribution to the overall rate and the rows add up to the total.

-- ==== Code ====
Produced Qty =
SUM ( 'Fact Output'[QtyProduced] )

Scrap Qty =
SUM ( 'Fact Scrap'[ScrapQty] )

-- Blank means 'no scrap booked'. If you need an explicit 0 percent on a card, wrap this one measure in IF ( [Produced Qty] > 0, COALESCE ( ..., 0 ) )
-- but not the base measure, otherwise every reason without scrap appears with 0 in a table.
Scrap Rate =
DIVIDE ( [Scrap Qty], [Produced Qty] )

Scrap ppm =
[Scrap Rate] * 1000000

-- Cost at standard cost of the product; RELATED works because 'Fact Scrap' is on the many side of Dim Product
Scrap Cost =
SUMX ( 'Fact Scrap', 'Fact Scrap'[ScrapQty] * RELATED ( 'Dim Product'[StandardCost] ) )

-- Share of each reason inside the current selection (machine, product, date); the reason filter is cleared, nothing else
Scrap Share of Reasons =
DIVIDE ( [Scrap Qty], CALCULATE ( [Scrap Qty], REMOVEFILTERS ( 'Dim Scrap Reason' ) ) )

-- Example target, set your own. Rounding before the comparison avoids floating point noise at the limit.
Scrap Target =
0.03

Scrap Status =
VAR Raw = [Scrap Rate]
RETURN
    IF ( ISBLANK ( Raw ), BLANK (), IF ( ROUND ( Raw, 5 ) > [Scrap Target], "Above target", "Within target" ) )

-- Worst machine first; only on machine rows, blank on subtotals and the total
Scrap Rate Rank (machine) =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Machine'[Machine] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Machine'[Machine] ), [Scrap Rate], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- Machine A makes Product P1 (standard cost 12.50), Machine B makes P2 (standard cost 30.00). One month.
--   Produced: A 15000, B 5000, total 20000
--   Scrap A: Dimension out of tolerance 180, Surface defect 120, Porosity 60 = 360
--   Scrap B: Dimension out of tolerance 40, Surface defect 200, Setup scrap 40 = 280
--   Scrap Rate: A = 360 / 15000 = 2.40%;  B = 280 / 5000 = 5.60%;  total = 640 / 20000 = 3.20%
--   Average of the two machine rates = 4.00%: wrong, because Machine B made only a quarter of the units.
--   Scrap Cost: A = 360 x 12.50 = 4,500.00;  B = 280 x 30.00 = 8,400.00;  total = 12,900.00
--   Scrap Rank (machine): B = 1, A = 2; the total row is blank. Status with target 3.0 percent: A within target, B above target. A rate exactly equal to the target counts as within target because the test is >.
-- Share of reasons in the total row selection (all machines): Dimension 34.4%, Surface defect 50.0%, Porosity 9.4%, Setup scrap 6.2%.
-- With Machine A selected by a slicer: Dimension 50.0%, Surface defect 33.3%, Porosity 16.7%. The share follows the selection
--   because REMOVEFILTERS touches only the reason table.
-- Scrap Rate per reason with Machine A selected: Dimension 1.20%, Surface defect 0.80%, Porosity 0.40%; they add up to 2.40%.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- If scrap is booked on the same table as production (one row per lot with a ScrapQty column), the model is simpler: use two SUM measures
--   and keep the share measure only if you have a reason dimension.
-- Rework: model it as its own quantity and rate; do not mix rework into scrap.
-- Customer returns and supplier rejects belong in separate facts; they have different dates and different owners.
-- Scrap in a rolling window: wrap [Scrap Qty] and [Produced Qty] in the same CALCULATE ( ..., DATESINPERIOD ( ... ) ) and divide afterwards.
-- Use the actual cost of the lot when you have it; standard cost makes machines comparable but ignores material price variance.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- Both facts are filtered through the same small dimensions; keep the dimension columns used in visuals low in cardinality.
-- SUMX with RELATED touches only the scrap rows, which are far fewer than the production rows.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- ALL ( 'Fact Scrap' ) or ALL ( 'Dim Scrap Reason' ) for the denominator of the share: ALL clears filters coming from Machine, Product and Date too.
--   REMOVEFILTERS on the one table whose filter you want to drop is the safe form.
-- Averaging the machine rates in a total row, or computing the rate as a calculated column and averaging it.
-- Putting the reason on the rows and being surprised that produced quantity does not change: that is the intended behaviour of this model.
-- Counting scrap in one unit (pieces) and produced quantity in another (kilograms).
-- Using the rank without ISINSCOPE: the total row then shows rank 1.
-- Forgetting that a rate with a blank numerator stays blank: machines without scrap vanish from a table unless you decide otherwise.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Scrap data is product and process data. If a lot record carries the operator or inspector, leave that column out of this model
--   and discuss with the works council before scrap figures are shown per person.
-- In aerospace, scrap, rework and concession decisions are controlled by the quality system and by authorised staff; this report
--   does not replace nonconformance records.

title: MTBF, MTTR and inherent availability in DAX across a production fact and a downtime fact
summary: DAX measures for MTBF, MTTR and inherent availability on two facts that share machine and date dimensions, with sum-first totals, blank handling for machines without failures and a rolling three-month MTBF.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- MTBF (mean time between failures), MTTR (mean time to repair) and inherent availability on a model with two facts: production
-- (operating time) and downtime events (failures and repair time). All divisions happen after the sums, so the total row is the
-- total operating time divided by the total number of failures, not an average of machine values. A rolling three-month MTBF sums
-- operating time and failures over the window first and divides second.
--   MTBF = operating time / number of failures        MTTR = repair time of failures / number of failures
--   Inherent availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)
-- Definitions differ between plants: this model counts rows flagged IsFailure as failures and uses RunMinutes as operating time. Write your definition next to the report.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact 1: 'Fact Production Shift'. GRAIN: one row per machine, per shift and day. Columns: Date, MachineKey, RunMinutes.
-- Fact 2: 'Fact Downtime'. GRAIN: one row per downtime event. Columns: EventID, Date (date the event STARTED), MachineKey, Minutes,
--   IsFailure (1 = unplanned breakdown that needed repair, 0 = other stop such as setup or waiting).
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date, Year, MonthNumber, YearMonth; marked as date table), 'Dim Machine' (MachineKey, Machine, Line, Plant).
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many and single direction: 'Dim Date'[Date] -> both facts' Date, 'Dim Machine'[MachineKey] -> both facts' MachineKey.
--   The two facts are never joined to each other; they meet only through the shared dimensions, which is what makes the cross-fact ratios work.
-- An event that runs over midnight is booked on its start date; for exact splitting do it in the source (see the KQL entry on MTBF and MTTR).

-- ==== Code ====
Operating Hours =
SUM ( 'Fact Production Shift'[RunMinutes] ) / 60

Failures =
CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Fact Downtime' ), 'Fact Downtime'[IsFailure] = 1 )

Repair Minutes =
CALCULATE ( SUM ( 'Fact Downtime'[Minutes] ), 'Fact Downtime'[IsFailure] = 1 )

-- Blank when there was no failure: there is no finite MTBF. Do not turn it into 0.
MTBF (h) =
DIVIDE ( [Operating Hours], [Failures] )

MTTR (min) =
DIVIDE ( [Repair Minutes], [Failures] )

Inherent Availability =
VAR MtbfMin = [MTBF (h)] * 60
VAR Mttr    = [MTTR (min)]
RETURN
    IF ( NOT ISBLANK ( MtbfMin ) && NOT ISBLANK ( Mttr ), DIVIDE ( MtbfMin, MtbfMin + Mttr ) )

-- Rolling three months ending at the last visible date: sum both parts over the window, then divide.
-- The window is only complete when three months of data exist; check the first months of a new model.
MTBF 3M (h) =
VAR Window = DATESINPERIOD ( 'Dim Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Dim Date'[Date] ), -3, MONTH )
VAR OperatingInWindow = CALCULATE ( [Operating Hours], Window )
VAR FailuresInWindow  = CALCULATE ( [Failures], Window )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( OperatingInWindow, FailuresInWindow )

-- Worst repair time first, only on machine rows
MTTR Rank (machine) =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Machine'[Machine] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Machine'[Machine] ), [MTTR (min)], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- Run minutes per month (Jan, Feb, Mar 2026): M1 [9000, 9600, 9300], M2 [9500, 9400, 9700], M3 [8000, 8200, 8100].
-- Failures (count, repair minutes) per month: M1 [(2, 120), (0, 0), (1, 90)], M2 [(1, 45), (1, 60), (0, 0)], M3 none.
-- Whole quarter:
--   M1     Operating h=465.0  Failures=3  Repair min=210  MTBF h=155.00  MTTR min=70.0  Inherent availability=99.25%
--   M2     Operating h=476.7  Failures=2  Repair min=105  MTBF h=238.33  MTTR min=52.5  Inherent availability=99.63%
--   M3     Operating h=405.0  Failures=0  Repair min=0  MTBF h=blank  MTTR min=blank  Inherent availability=blank
--   Total  Operating h=1346.7  Failures=5  Repair min=315  MTBF h=269.33  MTTR min=63.0  Inherent availability=99.61%
-- The total row: 1346.7 operating hours / 5 failures = 269.33 h. The average of the two machine MTBF values would be 196.67 h and ignores
--   that M3 ran 405.0 hours without a failure; the sum-first total includes those hours correctly.
-- Rolling three months at March, M1: (9000 + 9600 + 9300) / 60 = 465.0 h operating, 3 failures, MTBF 3M = 155.00 h.
-- Month view for M1: January MTBF = 75.0 h (2 failures), February blank (0 failures), March 155.0 h (1 failure). A chart of monthly MTBF
--   jumps around with so few failures; the rolling measure is the one to trend.
-- MTTR Rank (machine): M1 = 1 (70.0 min), M2 = 2 (52.5 min), M3 blank (no failures); the total row is blank.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Operating time from state data instead of production rows: take run minutes from your OEE fact; keep the same names.
-- Failures by cause: add a reason dimension to 'Fact Downtime' and use it on rows; MTBF by cause needs a definition (operating time is
--   not split by cause), so usually show failure count and repair time by cause and MTBF per machine.
-- Different failure definition: change the IsFailure flag in the source, not the measures.
-- Show 'no failure' text in cards: IF ( [Failures] = 0, "no failure", FORMAT ( [MTBF (h)], "0.0" ) ).
-- Targets: compare MTBF 3M with a target from your maintenance strategy; use ROUND before comparing.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- Both facts are filtered by the same two small dimensions; the measures are simple aggregations and cheap.
-- DATESINPERIOD works on the date table column, which is why the date table must be complete and marked.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Averaging MTBF values of machines or of months. Sum operating time and failures first.
-- Showing 0 for MTBF when there were no failures; DIVIDE returns blank, keep it.
-- Counting every downtime row as a failure although setups and waiting are in the same table: use IsFailure.
-- Using calendar hours as operating time for some machines and run hours for others.
-- A date table that ends in the future: MAX of the date column then moves the rolling window beyond the data and returns blank.
--   Limit the date table to the data range or derive the window end from the last date with data.
-- Reading MTBF from two failures as if it were a stable number.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Machine data, no personal data. Free-text fault descriptions can contain names; keep them out of the dataset or clean them.
-- In aerospace and MRO the maintenance records of aircraft and components are controlled records. This model is for shop equipment
--   reliability and does not replace maintenance programme data or release records.

title: First pass yield and rolled throughput yield in DAX with PRODUCTX and a reconciliation check
summary: DAX measures for FPY per process step and RTY across steps with PRODUCTX, an ISINSCOPE guard against misleading step rows, protection against missing steps and a reconciliation measure.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- First Pass Yield (FPY) per process step and Rolled Throughput Yield (RTY) across all steps.
--   FPY of a step = units that passed that step the first time, without rework or repair / units that entered the step
--   RTY = product of the FPY of all steps of the process = chance that a unit passes every step first time (under the stated assumption)
-- A reconciliation measure checks that first pass + rework + scrap equals the units in; if it does not, the yield is wrong and the
-- source data (not the DAX) has to be fixed. RTY uses PRODUCTX over the steps in the current selection, returns blank if a step has no
-- data (a missing step would otherwise be skipped silently and inflate RTY) and is blank on step rows because ISINSCOPE shows it is not the right figure there.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact Inspection'. GRAIN: one row per lot (or work order) and process step with the first inspection result. Columns: Date,
--   ProductKey, OperationKey, UnitsIn (units that entered the step for the first time), UnitsFirstPass (passed without rework or repair),
--   UnitsRework (needed rework or repair and were then accepted or are still in rework), UnitsScrap.
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Product' (ProductKey, PartNumber, Family), 'Dim Operation' (OperationKey,
--   Operation, Sequence). Keep one row per step in 'Dim Operation' and give the label a sort number so steps appear in process order.
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many, single direction: each dimension to 'Fact Inspection'.
-- Units that return from rework are not counted again in UnitsIn of the same step; otherwise FPY is understated.

-- ==== Code ====
Units In =
SUM ( 'Fact Inspection'[UnitsIn] )

Units First Pass =
SUM ( 'Fact Inspection'[UnitsFirstPass] )

FPY =
DIVIDE ( [Units First Pass], [Units In] )

-- Must be 0 in every cell; anything else means the lot data does not add up
Unreconciled Units =
[Units In]
    - ( SUM ( 'Fact Inspection'[UnitsFirstPass] ) + SUM ( 'Fact Inspection'[UnitsRework] ) + SUM ( 'Fact Inspection'[UnitsScrap] ) )

Steps with Data =
COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Dim Operation'[Operation] ), NOT ISBLANK ( [FPY] ) ) )

Steps in Selection =
COUNTROWS ( VALUES ( 'Dim Operation'[Operation] ) )

-- RTY: product of the step yields in the current selection of steps.
-- On a row of a single step the value would simply repeat that step's FPY, so it is blank there (ISINSCOPE),
-- and blank when a step of the selection has no data.
RTY =
IF (
    NOT ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Operation'[Operation] ) && [Steps with Data] = [Steps in Selection],
    PRODUCTX ( VALUES ( 'Dim Operation'[Operation] ), [FPY] )
)

-- Example target, set your own; the comparison uses rounded values
FPY Target =
0.95

FPY Status =
VAR Raw = [FPY]
RETURN
    IF ( ISBLANK ( Raw ), BLANK (), IF ( ROUND ( Raw, 4 ) >= [FPY Target], "At or above target", "Below target" ) )

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- One product, one month, three steps (one row per step shown as totals of its lots):
--   10 Machining           UnitsIn=1000  FirstPass=950  Rework=30  Scrap=20  FPY=950/1000=95.00%
--   20 Surface treatment   UnitsIn=980  FirstPass=931  Rework=40  Scrap=9  FPY=931/980=95.00%
--   30 Final inspection    UnitsIn=971  FirstPass=942  Rework=25  Scrap=4  FPY=942/971=97.01%
-- Unreconciled Units is 0 in each row. RTY = 95.00% x 95.00% x 97.01% = 87.55% on the total row of a visual with Operation on rows.
--   The average of the three FPY values would be 95.67%, which overstates the yield of the whole process.
-- With a target of 95 percent: step 10 is exactly 95.00 percent and counts as 'At or above target' because the test uses >=; step 20 also
--   (95.00 percent). The boundary is deliberate: write it into the definition sheet. Step 30 is 97.01%.
-- On a card with no Operation field in scope RTY shows 87.55%. On the three step rows RTY is blank and FPY shows the step values.
-- If the data for step 20 were missing, Steps with Data would be 2 and Steps in Selection 3, and RTY would show blank instead of the
--   misleading product of the other two steps.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Different units per step (a step that works on batches or panels): convert to the same unit in the source before loading.
-- Step names that repeat (two inspections of the same type): give each step its own key and sequence.
-- End-to-end yield from serial numbers: if you have unit-level history, count units that never had rework or scrap anywhere and divide
--   by units started; that is more exact than RTY, which multiplies step yields and assumes the steps are independent.
-- Filter by product: put Family or PartNumber on a slicer; RTY then covers only the steps with data for that product.
-- Add defects per unit or DPMO only if your quality system defines opportunities per unit; do not invent opportunity counts.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- PRODUCTX iterates the few steps of the process, and each step evaluates two sums; the cost is negligible.
-- The reconciliation measure is cheap enough to keep in a hidden check page of the report.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Counting reworked units as passed in FPY. That is the definition of final yield, not first pass yield.
-- Averaging the FPY values of the steps, or of the months, instead of multiplying across steps and summing units across months.
-- Letting RTY show on single-step rows, where it silently equals FPY and is mistaken for the process yield.
-- Missing steps: PRODUCTX ignores blanks, so a step without data would raise the RTY. The guard prevents this.
-- Units entering a step more than once (after rework) counted again in UnitsIn.
-- Comparing 94.999 percent with 95 percent without rounding.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Inspection counts are product data, not personal data. Do not add inspector names to this model if it is shared widely.
-- In aerospace, inspection results, nonconformances and release decisions are controlled by the quality system and by authorised staff;
--   this model is for yield analysis and does not replace inspection records.

title: Supplier on-time delivery and OTIF in DAX with explicit due-date and tolerance rules
summary: DAX measures for OTD and OTIF on purchase order lines that count only lines already due, handle tolerance days and open overdue lines, with boundary cases worked out and an ISINSCOPE-guarded supplier rank.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- On-time delivery (OTD) and on-time-in-full (OTIF) for supplier purchase order lines, with an explicit rule about which lines
-- are already 'decided'. A line counts in the measurement only when its promised date plus the tolerance lies BEFORE the as-of date.
-- Lines that are not yet due do not count, whether they are still open or were received early; otherwise an incomplete month looks
-- better than it is because only the early deliveries appear. A line promised today is not due until tomorrow.
--   OTD = lines that are due and were received on or before promised date + tolerance / lines that are due
--   OTIF = the same, and received quantity >= ordered quantity

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact PO Line'. GRAIN: one row per purchase order schedule line (one promised date and quantity). Columns: POLineID,
--   SupplierKey, PartKey, PromisedDate (date, no time), ReceiptDate (date of goods receipt; blank while open), OrderedQty, ReceivedQty.
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Supplier' (SupplierKey, Supplier, Country, Category), 'Dim Part' (PartKey, PartNumber).
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many, single direction: 'Dim Supplier'[SupplierKey] -> fact, 'Dim Part'[PartKey] -> fact,
--   'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] ACTIVE (the report period is the promised month), and optionally
--   'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact PO Line'[ReceiptDate] INACTIVE, used only with USERELATIONSHIP if you also report goods receipts per month.
-- Both date columns must be real dates; a time part would make 'received on the promised day' late.
-- Partial deliveries: if a schedule line is delivered in parts, either load one row per delivery or take the receipt date of the last part
--   and the total received quantity; decide and document it.

-- ==== Code ====
-- The as-of date: TODAY() in production. A measure so that you can replace it by a fixed date for testing or for month-end snapshots.
As Of Date =
TODAY ()

-- Grace days allowed beyond the promised date (0 = same day or earlier). Example value, set it from your supplier agreement.
OTD Tolerance Days =
0

-- Measure values are copied into variables first, so the row-by-row test below compares plain values.
PO Lines Due =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
VAR Tolerance = [OTD Tolerance Days]
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( 'Fact PO Line' ),
        FILTER ( 'Fact PO Line', 'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] + Tolerance < AsOf )
    )

PO Lines On Time =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
VAR Tolerance = [OTD Tolerance Days]
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( 'Fact PO Line' ),
        FILTER (
            'Fact PO Line',
            'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] + Tolerance < AsOf
                && NOT ISBLANK ( 'Fact PO Line'[ReceiptDate] )
                && 'Fact PO Line'[ReceiptDate] <= 'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] + Tolerance
        )
    )

PO Lines On Time In Full =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
VAR Tolerance = [OTD Tolerance Days]
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( 'Fact PO Line' ),
        FILTER (
            'Fact PO Line',
            'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] + Tolerance < AsOf
                && NOT ISBLANK ( 'Fact PO Line'[ReceiptDate] )
                && 'Fact PO Line'[ReceiptDate] <= 'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] + Tolerance
                && 'Fact PO Line'[ReceivedQty] >= 'Fact PO Line'[OrderedQty]
        )
    )

OTD % =
DIVIDE ( [PO Lines On Time], [PO Lines Due] )

OTIF % =
DIVIDE ( [PO Lines On Time In Full], [PO Lines Due] )

-- Lines that are due and still open: the list for the expediter
PO Lines Open and Overdue =
VAR AsOf = [As Of Date]
VAR Tolerance = [OTD Tolerance Days]
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( 'Fact PO Line' ),
        FILTER ( 'Fact PO Line', 'Fact PO Line'[PromisedDate] + Tolerance < AsOf && ISBLANK ( 'Fact PO Line'[ReceiptDate] ) )
    )

-- Worst supplier first, only on supplier rows (blank on subtotals and total)
OTD Rank (supplier) =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Supplier'[Supplier] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Supplier'[Supplier] ), [OTD %], , ASC, Dense )
)

-- ==== Worked example (invented lines, verified by calculation; As Of Date = 10 March 2026, tolerance 0) ====
--    1  S1  promised 02 Mar  receipt 02 Mar   ordered 100  received 100
--    2  S1  promised 03 Mar  receipt 05 Mar   ordered  50  received  50
--    3  S1  promised 09 Mar  receipt open     ordered  80  received   0
--    4  S1  promised 10 Mar  receipt open     ordered  60  received   0
--    5  S1  promised 20 Mar  receipt 08 Mar   ordered  40  received  40
--    6  S2  promised 04 Mar  receipt 04 Mar   ordered 200  received 150
--    7  S2  promised 06 Mar  receipt 05 Mar   ordered  50  received  50
--    8  S2  promised 07 Mar  receipt 08 Mar   ordered  70  received  70
--    9  S2  promised 09 Mar  receipt 09 Mar   ordered  80  received  80
--   10  S2  promised 12 Mar  receipt open     ordered  30  received   0
-- Due lines (promised date before 10 March): 7. On time: 4. OTD = 4 / 7 = 57.1%.
--   S1: due 3, on time 1 = 33.3%;  S2: due 4, on time 3 = 75.0%.
--   OTIF = 3 / 7 = 42.9% (line 6 was on time but only 150 of 200 arrived).
-- Boundary cases on purpose: line 4 is promised today and open, so it is not due yet; line 5 arrived early for a March 20 promise and is not counted;
--   line 9 arrived on its promised day and is on time (receipt <= promised); line 3 is open and overdue and counts as late; line 8 is one day late.
-- With OTD Tolerance Days = 1: 5 due lines (lines 3 and 9 are promised 9 March, plus one day is 10 March, which is not before the as-of date, so both drop out), 4 on time
--   (line 8 now counts as on time). OTD = 4 / 5 = 80.0%.
-- Open and overdue with tolerance 0: line 3 only.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Customer OTD: the same pattern on sales order lines (PromisedDate becomes the confirmed delivery date, ReceiptDate the ship or delivery date).
-- Different agreements per supplier: put the tolerance on 'Dim Supplier' and use MAX or SELECTEDVALUE of it inside a row-level FILTER with RELATED.
-- Month-end snapshots: replace the As Of Date measure by a fixed date so that the figure does not change when the report is opened later.
-- Weighted by value: replace COUNTROWS by SUMX of line value; report both counts and value, they tell different stories.
-- Show late days: add a measure with AVERAGEX over late lines of (ReceiptDate - PromisedDate), and treat open lines separately.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- FILTER over the fact table inside CALCULATE is evaluated for the rows in the current selection; for tens of millions of lines add a
--   calculated column [IsDue] and [IsOnTime] at refresh time, at the price of a fixed tolerance.
-- Keep PromisedDate and ReceiptDate as date type, not datetime, for compression and to avoid time-of-day errors.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Counting not-yet-due lines in the denominator (open lines lower OTD) or only early lines in the numerator (OTD above reality).
-- Using < where the agreement says 'on or before': a delivery on the promised day then counts as late.
-- Putting a measure inside a Boolean CALCULATE filter; use a variable.
-- Using ReceiptDate on the active relationship to Dim Date: the report period then moves lines between months when they arrive.
-- Averaging supplier OTD percentages in the total row; use the counts.
-- Ignoring partial deliveries and unit differences when you report OTIF.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Supplier performance data is business data. Individual buyers should not be named in this model. In aerospace, supplier approval,
--   release status and certificates are controlled by the quality system; OTD is a logistics figure and does not release material.

title: Takt time versus actual cycle time per line in DAX with correct weighting over days
summary: DAX measures that compare takt time and actual cycle time per line using totals instead of averaged daily values, blank takt for mixed selections, a boundary-correct status and a count of lines slower than takt.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- Compares takt time (the pace the customer demands) with the actual cycle time of each line, correctly weighted over days.
--   Takt time = available production time / customer demand (same period, same unit)
--   Actual cycle time = time the line spent producing / units produced
-- Both are ratios of sums, so a two-day view uses total time over total units and not the average of two daily values. Takt is only
-- meaningful for ONE line or one product flow, so it returns blank when several lines are in the selection (HASONEVALUE), and a
-- separate measure counts how many lines are slower than takt in the current selection. A status measure uses <= because a cycle
-- time equal to takt still meets demand.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact Line Day'. GRAIN: one row per production line and calendar day. Columns: Date, LineKey, AvailableSeconds (planned production
--   time of the day minus breaks and planned stops, in seconds), DemandUnits (customer demand the line must serve that day, in units),
--   UnitsProduced (good units made), ProducingSeconds (time the line was actually making units, excluding stops).
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Line' (LineKey, Line, Plant, Product Family).
-- RELATIONSHIPS: 'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact Line Day'[Date]; 'Dim Line'[LineKey] -> 'Fact Line Day'[LineKey]; both one-to-many, single direction.
-- If one line makes several products with different cycle times, add ProductKey to the grain and compare per product; one takt per mixed
--   line is not meaningful.

-- ==== Code ====
Available Seconds =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[AvailableSeconds] )

Demand Units =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[DemandUnits] )

Units Produced =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[UnitsProduced] )

Producing Seconds =
SUM ( 'Fact Line Day'[ProducingSeconds] )

-- Takt only for a single line in scope; blank for several lines, because adding up available time of lines that make different
-- products and dividing by their demand mixes unlike things.
Takt Time (s) =
IF ( HASONEVALUE ( 'Dim Line'[Line] ), DIVIDE ( [Available Seconds], [Demand Units] ) )

Cycle Time (s) =
IF ( HASONEVALUE ( 'Dim Line'[Line] ), DIVIDE ( [Producing Seconds], [Units Produced] ) )

-- Above 1.0: the line is slower than demand requires
Cycle to Takt Ratio =
DIVIDE ( [Cycle Time (s)], [Takt Time (s)] )

-- Units per hour the customer demand requires, and what the line actually delivers while producing
Required Units per Hour =
DIVIDE ( 3600, [Takt Time (s)] )

Line Capacity Units per Hour =
DIVIDE ( 3600, [Cycle Time (s)] )

Takt Status =
VAR Cycle = [Cycle Time (s)]
VAR Takt  = [Takt Time (s)]
RETURN
    IF ( ISBLANK ( Cycle ) || ISBLANK ( Takt ), BLANK (), IF ( ROUND ( Cycle, 2 ) <= ROUND ( Takt, 2 ), "Meets takt", "Slower than takt" ) )

-- Works for any selection: counts lines whose own cycle time is above their own takt. [Cycle Time (s)] and [Takt Time (s)]
-- are evaluated per line because the row context of VALUES turns into a filter on the line.
Lines Slower than Takt =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Dim Line'[Line] ), [Cycle Time (s)] > [Takt Time (s)] )
)

-- Share of the day's available time the line would need to meet demand at its measured cycle time (above 100 percent = not enough time)
Required Time Utilisation =
DIVIDE ( [Demand Units] * [Cycle Time (s)], [Available Seconds] )

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- Two days, two lines. Available time 27000 s per line and day (7.5 hours).
--   Line 1: day 1 demand 450, produced 450, producing 24300 s;  day 2 demand 300, produced 300, producing 18000 s
--   Line 2: day 1 demand 400, produced 380, producing 27000 s;  day 2 demand 380, produced 340, producing 27000 s
-- Line 1: takt = 54000 / 750 = 72.00 s. Daily takt would be 60.0 s and 90.0 s; their plain average is 75.0 s, which is wrong because the days carry different demand.
--   Cycle time = 42300 / 750 = 56.40 s (daily 54.0 s and 60.0 s; the plain average 57.0 s is wrong as well). Ratio 0.783: meets takt.
-- Line 2: takt = 54000 / 780 = 69.23 s. Cycle time = 54000 / 720 = 75.00 s. Ratio 1.083: slower than takt. Capacity 48.0 units/h against 52.0 required.
--   Required time utilisation = 780 x 75.00 / 54000 = 108.3%: the demand would need more than the available time.
-- Total row (both lines in scope): Takt Time and Cycle Time are blank; Lines Slower than Takt = 1.
-- Status uses <=: if a line's cycle time equals its takt exactly it meets takt.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Demand in your planning system may be weekly: aggregate to the day in the source or keep the grain and make sure available time uses the same period.
-- If your takt definition subtracts breaks and meetings, do that in AvailableSeconds in the source and document it.
-- Use cycle time from time studies or machine data for ProducingSeconds; if the line has several stations, the cycle time of the whole line
--   is determined by the slowest station (bottleneck), so keep station cycle times in a separate fact.
-- Add a product dimension if lines change over: the same logic works per product, and the line total then becomes blank by design.
-- Reduce to a card for one line: put Line in a slicer; HASONEVALUE is then true and the measures show.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- One fact, simple sums; the FILTER over VALUES ( Line ) iterates the number of lines, a handful.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Averaging daily takt or cycle values instead of dividing the summed times by the summed demand and units.
-- Showing one takt for several lines in one total row.
-- Mixing units: demand in pieces, production in kits.
-- Using produced units (including scrap) for cycle time while demand is in good units; say which one you use.
-- Using < instead of <= in the status: a line exactly at takt then looks like a gap.
-- Treating cycle time as equal to takt when the line is simply forced to wait; waiting is a loss, not the pace.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Line and demand data are business data, no personal data. Do not add operator names to this dataset; discuss with the works council how
--   line results may be used. Cycle times are planning figures and do not replace work instructions or approved process data.

title: Inventory turnover and days of inventory in DAX from month-end snapshots
summary: DAX measures for annualised inventory turns and days of inventory that treat stock as semi-additive: closing balance with LASTNONBLANK, average of month-end values and days limited to the data, with a checked example.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- Inventory turnover and days of inventory on a model with a month-end snapshot fact and a consumption fact.
--   Turns (annualised) = consumption value of the period / average inventory value x 365 / days in the period
--   Days of inventory = average inventory value / consumption value x days in the period
-- Stock is a semi-additive quantity: it can be added across parts but never across dates. The closing balance of a period is the
-- snapshot of its last date with data, and the average inventory is the average of the month-end balances in the period. Summing
-- the snapshot rows over a quarter would triple-count the stock.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact 1: 'Fact Inventory Snapshot'. GRAIN: one row per part and month-end snapshot date. Columns: SnapshotDate, PartKey, QtyOnHand, StockValue.
-- Fact 2: 'Fact Consumption'. GRAIN: one row per part and day. Columns: Date, PartKey, ConsumedValue (value of material issued to
--   production, or cost of goods sold, as defined in your finance policy).
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date, Year, MonthNumber, YearMonth text such as 2026-01; contiguous, one row per calendar day, marked as date table),
--   'Dim Part' (PartKey, PartNumber, Category, ABCClass).
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many, single direction: 'Dim Date'[Date] -> 'Fact Inventory Snapshot'[SnapshotDate] and -> 'Fact Consumption'[Date];
--   'Dim Part'[PartKey] -> both facts.
-- The turnover figure only makes sense with a full-year view or a stated period; one month gives a very noisy value.

-- ==== Code ====
Consumption Value =
SUM ( 'Fact Consumption'[ConsumedValue] )

-- Last snapshot with data inside the current date selection (the balance at the end of the period).
-- LASTNONBLANK handles an incomplete current month, where the last calendar day has no snapshot yet.
Closing Inventory Value =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( 'Fact Inventory Snapshot'[StockValue] ),
    LASTNONBLANK ( 'Dim Date'[Date], CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( 'Fact Inventory Snapshot' ) ) )
)

-- Average of the month-end balances of the months in the selection; months without a snapshot are skipped by AVERAGEX
Average Inventory Value =
AVERAGEX ( VALUES ( 'Dim Date'[YearMonth] ), [Closing Inventory Value] )

-- Last day with consumption data, ignoring every filter; REMOVEFILTERS () keeps part and date filters from changing it.
Last Consumption Date =
CALCULATE ( MAX ( 'Fact Consumption'[Date] ), REMOVEFILTERS () )

-- Days of the selection up to the last day with data, so a year in progress is not diluted by future days
Days in Period =
VAR LastData = [Last Consumption Date]
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( VALUES ( 'Dim Date'[Date] ), 'Dim Date'[Date] <= LastData ) )

Inventory Turns (annualised) =
DIVIDE ( [Consumption Value], [Average Inventory Value] ) * DIVIDE ( 365, [Days in Period] )

Days of Inventory =
DIVIDE ( [Average Inventory Value], [Consumption Value] ) * [Days in Period]

-- Turns rank across part categories; blank on the total row
Turns Rank (category) =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Part'[Category] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Part'[Category] ), [Inventory Turns (annualised)], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- ==== Worked example (invented numbers, verified by calculation) ====
-- January to March 2026 = 90 days. Month-end stock value and consumption value per part:
--   P1: stock [50000, 46000, 54000], consumption [30000, 28000, 31000]
--   P2: stock [20000, 24000, 22000], consumption [6000, 5000, 7000]
-- P1: average inventory = (50000 + 46000 + 54000) / 3 = 50000; consumption 89000; turns = 89000 / 50000 x 365 / 90 = 7.219; days of inventory = 50.6.
-- P2: average inventory = 22000; consumption 18000; turns = 3.318; days of inventory = 110.0.
-- Both parts (total row): month-end totals are 70000, 70000, 76000; average inventory 72000; consumption 107000; turns = 6.027; days of inventory = 60.6.
-- The wrong way: summing the three snapshots (216000) as 'inventory' would give turns of 2.009, three times too low.
-- If the report is opened on 15 April and consumption data ends on 31 March, Last Consumption Date stays 31 March and Days in Period for a
--   'year 2026' selection is 90, not 365.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Quarter or year: the same measures work; with more months the average inventory becomes more stable. Use at least twelve months for a yearly figure.
-- Quantity based turns: build the same pair with QtyOnHand and consumed quantity when parts are comparable in units.
-- Weekly snapshots: replace the YearMonth grouping column in Average Inventory Value by a week column of the date table.
-- Slow movers and obsolescence: add a measure for stock value of parts with no consumption in the last twelve months, defined in your inventory policy.
-- Aerospace spares: low turns can be intended (safety stock for rarely used rotables); use ABCClass or a criticality column on 'Dim Part' to compare like with like.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- AVERAGEX iterates months, not days; with a few years of data that is dozens of iterations, each with two small aggregations.
-- The snapshot table grows with parts times months; that is far smaller than a daily stock history.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Adding snapshot values across dates (a plain SUM over a quarter). Stock must be taken at a point in time and averaged.
-- Using LASTDATE instead of LASTNONBLANK and getting blank for the current month because the last calendar day has no snapshot yet.
-- Dividing by 365 days for a year in progress; use the days that have data.
-- Mixing consumption at cost with stock at a different valuation (standard cost vs moving average).
-- ALL ( 'Dim Date' ) in the last-date measure: it clears only the date filters, so a part filter still changes the result and every part gets its own last date.
--   REMOVEFILTERS () clears every filter, which is what 'last day with data in the whole model' means.
-- Reading a turns rank of one category without checking that the categories hold comparable parts.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Inventory and consumption values are business data without personal data. Stock valuations can be commercially sensitive; limit the dataset to the roles that need it.
-- In aerospace, serialised and shelf-life parts have traceability and release rules in the quality system; this model is a planning figure and
--   does not replace stores records or part traceability.

title: Downtime Pareto with a correct cumulative percentage line in DAX using ALLSELECTED and ISINSCOPE
summary: DAX measures for a downtime Pareto: ranked reasons, cumulative minutes with a tie-break, cumulative percent that follows slicers, blank totals via ISINSCOPE and a vital-few class with a clear 80 percent boundary rule.
body:
-- ==== What it does ====
-- A downtime Pareto with a correct cumulative percentage line. For every reason it adds up the minutes of all reasons that rank higher,
-- with a tie-break so that reasons with equal minutes get a stable order, and divides by the total of the current selection. The measures
-- return blank on subtotal and total rows (ISINSCOPE), because a cumulative value has no meaning there. ALLSELECTED on the reason column
-- ignores the rows of the visual but keeps slicers (machine, line, date, reason category), so the Pareto always describes the selection the user made.
-- A class measure marks the 'vital few' reasons: reasons that start below 80 percent of cumulative downtime, which includes the reason that crosses the 80 percent line.

-- ==== Required tables/columns (assumed star schema) ====
-- Fact: 'Fact Downtime'. GRAIN: one row per downtime event. Columns: EventID, Date (start date), MachineKey, ReasonKey, Minutes.
-- Dimensions: 'Dim Date' (Date; marked as date table), 'Dim Machine' (MachineKey, Machine, Line, Plant), 'Dim Downtime Reason'
--   (ReasonKey, Reason, Category). Reason must be unique per row of the dimension.
-- RELATIONSHIPS, one-to-many, single direction: each dimension to 'Fact Downtime'.
-- Visual: a combo chart with the reason on the axis, [Downtime Min] as columns and [Downtime Cumulative %] as a line on a secondary axis (0 to 100 percent),
--   sorted by [Downtime Min] descending. The sort of the visual is not done by DAX; set it in the visual. Equal values are ordered by name in the measure;
--   in the visual add a second sort by Reason ascending for the same order.

-- ==== Code ====
Downtime Min =
SUM ( 'Fact Downtime'[Minutes] )

-- Total of the visual: all reasons that are visible after slicers, regardless of the row of the visual
Downtime Total (selection) =
CALCULATE ( [Downtime Min], ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Downtime Reason' ) )

-- Minutes of this reason plus all reasons that rank above it. Rank order: more minutes first, equal minutes by name A to Z.
Downtime Cumulative Min =
VAR CurrentReason = SELECTEDVALUE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] )
VAR CurrentMin    = [Downtime Min]
VAR Reasons =
    ADDCOLUMNS ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ), "@Min", [Downtime Min] )
RETURN
    IF (
        ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ),
        SUMX (
            FILTER (
                Reasons,
                [@Min] > CurrentMin
                    || ( [@Min] = CurrentMin && 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] <= CurrentReason )
            ),
            [@Min]
        )
    )

Downtime Cumulative % =
DIVIDE ( [Downtime Cumulative Min], [Downtime Total (selection)] )

-- Rank 1 = largest loss; reasons with equal minutes share a rank (Dense). Blank on subtotals.
Downtime Rank =
IF (
    ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ),
    RANKX ( ALLSELECTED ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ), [Downtime Min], , DESC, Dense )
)

-- Class A = vital few. A reason is in class A when the cumulative share BEFORE it is below 80 percent (strictly), so that
-- the reason that carries the total across 80 percent is still included.
Downtime Pareto Class =
VAR ShareBefore =
    DIVIDE ( [Downtime Cumulative Min] - [Downtime Min], [Downtime Total (selection)] )
RETURN
    IF ( ISINSCOPE ( 'Dim Downtime Reason'[Reason] ) && NOT ISBLANK ( ShareBefore ), IF ( ShareBefore < 0.8, "A", "B/C" ) )

-- ==== Worked example (invented minutes, verified by calculation) ====
-- One month, all machines selected, total 1200 minutes. Sorted by minutes descending, ties by name:
--   Material shortage  Min=420  Cumulative min= 420  Cumulative %= 35.0%  Cum % before this reason=  0.0%  Class=A
--   Spindle fault      Min=310  Cumulative min= 730  Cumulative %= 60.8%  Cum % before this reason= 35.0%  Class=A
--   Operator absent    Min=180  Cumulative min= 910  Cumulative %= 75.8%  Cum % before this reason= 60.8%  Class=A
--   Tool change        Min=180  Cumulative min=1090  Cumulative %= 90.8%  Cum % before this reason= 75.8%  Class=A
--   Waiting for QA     Min= 90  Cumulative min=1180  Cumulative %= 98.3%  Cum % before this reason= 90.8%  Class=B/C
--   Other              Min= 20  Cumulative min=1200  Cumulative %=100.0%  Cum % before this reason= 98.3%  Class=B/C
-- Operator absent and Tool change both have 180 minutes. Without a tie-break both rows would get the same cumulative value, the line would show
--   a flat step and one of the two percentages would be wrong; with the name rule Operator absent comes first (cumulative 910) and Tool change second (1090).
-- Tool change starts at 75.8% (below 80 percent) and ends at 90.8%: it is class A because the share BEFORE it is below 80 percent.
--   Waiting for QA starts at 90.8% and is class B/C.
-- Downtime Rank: Material shortage 1, Spindle fault 2, Operator absent 3, Tool change 3, Waiting for QA 4, Other 5.
-- The total row of the visual shows blank for Cumulative Min, Cumulative %, Rank and Class; [Downtime Min] shows 1200.
-- Slicer check: select only the reason category 'Planned' in a slicer on Dim Downtime Reason and the Pareto is calculated over those reasons only,
--   because ALLSELECTED keeps the slicer; with a plain ALL on the reason table it would still include all reasons in the total.

-- ==== How to adapt ====
-- Group small reasons into 'Other': build the grouping in the dimension (a column ReasonGroup) and use that column in place of Reason in the measures.
-- Pareto by cost instead of minutes: replace [Downtime Min] by a cost measure everywhere; the structure stays the same.
-- Top N only: show rows where [Downtime Rank] <= 5 with a visual filter on the rank measure; the cumulative values are still computed over all visible reasons.
-- Change the 80 percent line to your own convention; the strict < at the boundary is a choice, write it into the definition.
-- Combine with a machine slicer to build a Pareto per machine; nothing in the measures is hard-coded to a machine.

-- ==== Performance notes ====
-- The measure iterates the reasons (dozens), and each iteration evaluates the base measure once; this is fast.
-- If you have hundreds of reasons, group them in the dimension first; a Pareto with 300 bars is not readable anyway.

-- ==== Common mistakes ====
-- Using ALL ( 'Dim Downtime Reason' ) to build the list of reasons: slicers on category are then ignored and the cumulative line does not reach 100 percent.
-- Forgetting the tie-break: reasons with equal minutes then get the same cumulative value or are skipped.
-- No ISINSCOPE guard: the total row shows a cumulative value that equals the grand total or a meaningless figure.
-- Putting the cumulative line on the same axis as the minutes; it must use a percent axis from 0 to 100.

-- ==== Privacy and safety ====
-- Downtime reasons are machine data. If operators select the reason, do not show results per operator; discuss with the works council how reason data may be used.
-- The Pareto points to where to look; the decision about corrective action remains with the responsible people. In aerospace and MRO, it does not replace maintenance or quality records.
